newsitem.title: UK: Old mattresses may increase cot death risk - study.
newsitem.headline: Old mattresses may increase cot death risk - study.

text.p: Putting babies to sleep on an old mattress may increase the risk of cot death, Scottish researchers said on Friday.
A study of 201 cases of sudden infant death syndrome in Scotland found that sleeping on a mattress previously used by another child or adult may be an additional factor behind infant deaths.
"The results from the mattress analysis were unexpected," said the report, published in the British Medical Journal.
However, the study also found that there appeared to be no risk from sleeping on mattresses covered with PVC.
This contradicts the view that PVC covers could themselves be a factor in cot deaths, with household fungi interacting with fire-retardant chemicals and releasing toxic gases.
"The failure to establish risk with mattresses completely covered with PVC may be because they can be kept clean, regardless of age, while others cannot," the study said.

However the scientists, from the Scottish Cot Death Trust, the University of Glasgow and the University of Edinburgh Medical School, said the findings needed confirmation before recommendations could be made to parents.
The English-based Foundation for the Study of Infant Deaths (FISD) said it was worried the study could unnecessarily alarm parents who could not afford new mattresses for each baby.
It said the preliminary findings of the study were found only for mattresses which were difficult to keep clean, mainly those with ventilation holes "which tend to be a sump for dribble and vomit."
The report "reinforces long-standing advice that mattresses must be kept clean," the foundation said.

Other findings by the Scottish researchers confirmed what are now widely accepted as being major risk factors in cot deaths. They said smoking by parents is currently the most significant controllable risk, and that bed-sharing with an infant should be discouraged if the mother smokes.
The study also repeated advice first established in New Zealand that babies should be put to bed on their backs rather than on their front or side.

In a reminder of standard advice to parents worried about cot deaths, the secretary-general of the FISD Joyce Epstein said "it is obvious that clean mattresses are preferable to dirty ones. Parents who have their baby on a clean mattress need not rush out to buy a new one. The important messages to remember are: sleep babies on their backs, don't smoke around them, ensure they don't overheat...and seek medical advice if you are worried about their health."
